changeLog.note: Editorial rewrite of advisor and client prose; substance unchanged.

advisor.summary: Section 162(l) hands self-employed taxpayers — Schedule C proprietors, partners, and more-than-2% S corporation shareholders — an above-the-line deduction for health, dental, and age-capped long-term-care premiums covering the owner, spouse, dependents, and children under 27. Two guardrails drive the planning: the deduction cannot exceed earned income from the business sponsoring the plan, and it is lost for any month in which either spouse was merely eligible for a subsidized employer plan, enrolled or not. S corporation owners reach the deduction only through the Notice 2008-1 mechanics — the corporation pays or reimburses the premium and includes it in the shareholder's Box 1 W-2 wages — so a premium paid from a personal checking account with no payroll add-back yields nothing. The deduction reduces income tax but not self-employment tax, and premiums the §36B premium tax credit already covered cannot be deducted a second time. In practice this is housekeeping rather than an aggressive position: the most common failure is a deduction never claimed, or parked on Schedule A where the 7.5% AGI floor swallows it.
mechanics: The deduction sits above the line on Schedule 1, computed on Form 7206 — no itemizing, no 7.5% AGI floor — and covers medical and dental premiums plus qualified long-term-care premiums up to the age-indexed dollar caps, for the taxpayer, spouse, dependents, and children not yet 27 (§162(l)(1), §162(l)(2)(C)).

Earned income from the sponsoring trade or business caps the deduction: Schedule C profit less half of SE tax and SE retirement contributions, or, for a >2% S corporation shareholder, W-2 wages from that corporation (§162(l)(2)(A)); excess premium falls to Schedule A behind the 7.5% floor.

Because §1372 treats >2% S corporation shareholders as partners for fringe-benefit purposes, the premium must route through the corporation: the entity pays or reimburses it and adds the amount to Box 1 wages (exempt from FICA), and the shareholder then deducts it under §162(l) per Notice 2008-1 — the whole deduction turns on this payroll routing.

Eligibility is tested month by month: no deduction for any calendar month in which the taxpayer or the spouse could have participated in a subsidized employer health plan (§162(l)(2)(B)); declining the employer's offer does not restore the month.

The deduction and the §36B premium tax credit cannot claim the same dollars — only the net, unsubsidized premium is deductible — and because each figure feeds the other, exchange-policy clients need the iterative or simplified computation of Rev. Proc. 2014-41.

The benefit is income tax only: §1402 leaves the deduction out of the SE-tax computation, and the deduction attributable to the business also trims qualified business income for §199A purposes — the model reflects both.

authority.note: The deduction: covered premiums and family members, the earned-income cap in (2)(A), and the month-by-month subsidized-employer-eligibility disallowance in (2)(B).
The S corporation pathway: premiums the corporation pays or reimburses and includes in the >2% shareholder's Box 1 W-2 wages qualify for §162(l); premiums paid personally with no add-back do not.
Treats >2% S corporation shareholders as partners for fringe benefits — why the premium lands in W-2 wages rather than staying an excludable benefit.
The premium tax credit; §162(l) reaches only what the credit did not pay, blocking a double benefit on exchange coverage.
The iterative and simplified methods for computing the §162(l) deduction and §36B credit together, each being an input to the other.
The computation form that implements the deduction and its earned-income limit.
Net earnings from self-employment are figured without subtracting the §162(l) deduction — the benefit is income tax only.
The deduction attributable to the business reduces qualified business income, trimming the 20% deduction alongside the income-tax savings.

requirements: Positive earned income from the sponsoring business: Schedule C net profit, K-1 self-employment earnings, or S corporation W-2 wages for a >2% shareholder.

A plan established under the business — for Schedule C, a policy in the owner's or the business's name; for an S corporation, corporate payment or reimbursement plus Box 1 W-2 inclusion before the year's final payroll.
No month claimed in which either spouse was eligible for subsidized employer coverage.
For exchange policies carrying a premium tax credit, the coordinated Rev. Proc. 2014-41 computation.
No overlap with a §105 reimbursement plan — each premium dollar is deducted once.
risks: The leading exam theory is mechanical disallowance, not a litigated doctrine: an S corporation owner who paid premiums personally without the Notice 2008-1 payroll add-back has no plan established under the business, and the deduction fails in full — a foot-fault cheap to fix before year-end payroll closes and expensive to discover after.
Months claimed while a spouse's employer offered subsidized coverage are disallowed on eligibility alone; enrollment is irrelevant, and examiners verify this item first.
The earned-income cap means a loss-year business supports no deduction; the excess survives only on Schedule A above the 7.5% floor — usually meaning not at all.
Deducting premiums the premium tax credit effectively paid is a double benefit; the Rev. Proc. 2014-41 computation exists precisely to police that line.
Running the same premiums through both §162(l) and a §105 spouse-employee plan double-counts the deduction.
stateNotes: Conformity: states starting from federal AGI absorb the §162(l) deduction automatically; confirm treatment in decoupled or gross-income-start states in the client's footprint before projecting a state benefit.

PTET interaction: §162(l) is a personal above-the-line deduction and does not reduce the base on which a pass-through entity tax is computed. For S corporation owners, the premium add-back is already a wage deduction inside the entity's ordinary income, so the entity-level effect flows through the K-1 — do not adjust the PTET base twice.

Missouri: conforms through the federal AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121) with no addback. Watch the interplay with Missouri's separate health-premium subtraction (RSMo §143.113): it reaches only premiums not already deducted federally, so dollars claimed under §162(l) cannot be subtracted again on the MO-1040.
reviewChecklist: Earned-income cap computed; deduction confirmed not to exceed it.
Policy verified as established under the business; for S corporation clients, Box 1 W-2 inclusion confirmed on the year's final payroll.
Month-by-month subsidized-employer-eligibility check completed for both spouses.
Rev. Proc. 2014-41 computation run for any exchange policy carrying a premium tax credit; Form 1095-A in the file.
Medicare premiums captured for owners 65+, and no month claimed after Medicare disqualification issues arise on companion strategies.
No premium dollar claimed under a §105 plan or anywhere else.

client.teaser: You already pay for health insurance — set up right, every dollar can lower your taxable income.
client.headline: Turn your health insurance bill into a full deduction.
plainEnglish: When you work for yourself, the health insurance you pay for — for you, your spouse, and your kids — can come off your income before tax is figured. Dental premiums count. Long-term-care premiums count. Even Medicare premiums can count.

Many owners miss part or all of this. If you own an S corporation, the premiums must flow through the company and show up on your W-2 in a set way. Paid the wrong way, the whole deduction can be lost. That is a payroll fix, not an insurance change, and doing it right costs nothing.

There are limits. The deduction cannot be more than the business earns. And it shuts off for any month you or your spouse could have joined an employer's subsidized plan — even if you said no. We check each month, fix the payroll handling, and make sure the full amount holds up.
client.analogy: Think of a coupon printed on a bill you have paid for years without seeing it. The premium stays the same — but claimed the right way, the tax law hands part of it back every year.
benefits: Premiums come off your income directly — no itemizing needed.
Health, dental, long-term-care, and Medicare premiums can all count.
Family coverage qualifies, including children under 27.
Usually just a paperwork fix — your insurance does not change.
steps: WE list every premium your household pays and who pays it.
WE check the eligibility rules month by month so the deduction holds up.
WE set up the S corporation payroll handling before year-end, if that applies to you.
YOU send us your premium statements and tell us about any employer coverage offered to you or your spouse.
YOU pay business premiums from the company account, not your personal one.
clientCommitments: Tell us right away if you or your spouse is offered coverage at a job, even if you turn it down.
For S corporation owners: let the company pay or repay the premiums so they reach your W-2 the right way.
Send us Form 1095-A each year if your coverage comes from the exchange.
Keep premium statements so every amount can be backed up.

Month-by-month employer-coverage eligibility recheck for both spouses.
Premium tax credit coordination recomputed whenever exchange coverage is present.
